Occasionally, we wish to find the maximum or minimum of a function subject to a constraint. The solution is to use Lagrange multipliers. Suppose we wish to find the extrema of a function, $ f() $, subject to the constraint that $ h() = c $. We first construct a new function by considering $$ g(\mathbf{x},\lambda)=f(\mathbf{x})-\lambda[h(\mathbf{x})-c] $$ Because $ h() - c = 0 $, the extrema of $ g(,) $ correspond to the extrema of $ f() $ under the constraint. Local maxima and minima are obtained by solving the following set of equations: $$ 
abla_{\mathbf{x}}[g(\mathbf{x},\lambda)]=
abla_{\mathbf{x}}[f(\mathbf{x})]-\lambda\cdot
abla_{\mathbf{x}}[h(\mathbf{x})]=\mathbf{0} $$ $$  rac{d g(\mathbf{x},\lambda)}{d\lambda}=h(\mathbf{x})-c=0 $$
Observe that the second equation is satisfied by the constraint.

Example A6.8. A standard approach for selection on multiple traits is to use a selection index, I, which is a new (univariate) trait that is a linear combination of n characters $ = (z_1, z_2,, z_n)^T $, with $$ I=\mathbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{z}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}b_{k}z_{k} $$

Notice that what matters for the weights are their relative proportions, as, if we were to multiply all of the weights by the same constant (e.g., $ a_ b_k $), this new index would still choose the same individuals. Hence, to obtain a standardized index, we impose the constraint $ ^T = 1 $. We denote the directional selection differential on the index by $ S_I $, and observe that if $ $ is the vector of directional selection differentials generated by selecting on $ I $, then $ S_I = ^T $.

Smith (1936) and Hazel (1943) showed that a larger response in a target index is obtained by selecting on a different index. Suppose our aim is to maximize the response in the index, $$ J=\mathbf{a}^{T}\boldsymbol{\mu}=\sum a_{k}\mu_{k} $$

What are the standardized weights, b, for the optimal Smith-Hazel index (for a fixed amount of selection, $ S_I = s $? If we assume that the conditions leading to the multivariate breeder's equation hold, the function to maximize is $$ f(\mathbf{b})=\mathbf{a}^{T} oldsymbol{\Delta} oldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{a}^{T}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{a}^{T}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{S} $$ under the associated constraint function $$ g(\mathbf{b})-c=\mathbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{b}-1=0 $$ Because $S_I = b^T S$, and we have the constraint that $b^T b = 1$, set $S = s b$, so that $S_I = b^T S = s b^T b = s$. If we use these functions, Equation A6.10a yields $$  egin{aligned}

abla_{\mathbf{b}}[\mathbf{a}^{T}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{b}]-\lambda\cdot

Note that the constant $ 2 /s $ simply standardizes the weights (so that $ ^T =1 $), and hence the Smith-Hazel weights are usually written as $$ \mathbf{b}_{SH}=\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{G}^{T}\mathbf{a} $$ which can be standardized by noting that $$ \mathbf{b}=\frac{\mathbf{b}_{SH}}{\left|\left|\mathbf{b}_{SH}\right|\right|}=\frac{\mathbf{b}_{SH}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{b}_{SH}^{T}\mathbf{b}_{SH}}} $$
